scope: Hays expansion Phase 2 second eight diagnostic packet, separate from first eight
source_evidence: Original 1999 Flora PDF searched directly from user Library for treatment pages. Hays photo-visible notes and source IDs reused from earlier saved visual QA, NOT re-inspected today. Hill Country descriptions sourced from saved regional crosswalk. No new photos viewed.
photo_license_rule: Preflight rights lane only; publisher/photo-credit recheck plus intended use determination before publishing. NO images copied or rehosted.
distinctions: Descriptions reflect literature taxa, not verification of pictured Hays specimens. Empty Lab key states mean unknown, not absent. Two records have no rights-safe visual review.

source_key.reference: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon, Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas (1999)

taxa.hill_country_key: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), Grasses of the Texas Hill Country: Vegetative Key and Descriptions; individual characters labeled when used

source_supported_morphology.description: Annual, generally 35–75 cm tall
Leaf sheaths mostly hairless apart from margins; blade base may flare into small auricles
Membranous, shorter than 1 mm
Slender cylindrical spike with spikelets fitting niches along an unbranched flattened, bilaterally organized axis
Sessile spikelets with 2–5 florets; upper florets often reduced
Glumes and lemmas of upper spikelets bear long awns, approximately 3–8 cm

taxa.actually_visible_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Good views of slender jointed cylindrical spike; detached spike segments/units and auricle-area photos visible.
taxa.not_demonstrated_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Glume arrangement, exact joint/awn dimensions and competing Aegilops species not measured.
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Photograph one intact ripe spike and detached spike joint/spikelet on a millimeter scale, exposing glumes, floret count, ligule and auricle.
taxa.lookalikes: Hordeum spp., Triticum aestivum and other Aegilops
taxa.caution: Photo architecture strongly supports jointed goatgrass but not independently verified species anatomy; confirm spontaneous roadside occurrence.

source_key.reference: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon, Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas (1999)

taxa.hill_country_key: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), Grasses of the Texas Hill Country: Vegetative Key and Descriptions; individual characters labeled when used

source_supported_morphology.description: Tufted, hard-based perennial, usually 15–75 cm tall
Sheaths mostly hairless except margins and the uppermost opening
Open panicle with visibly sticky/viscid axis, often detaching with age
Narrow leaf blades may project abruptly outward, near a right angle
Very short fringe of hairs rather than a prominent long membrane

taxa.actually_visible_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Single open and diffuse lovegrass-like panicle image.
taxa.not_demonstrated_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Crucial viscid/gummy panicle axis cannot be demonstrated; mature spikelet dimensions not visible.
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Obtain a sharp same-plant macro demonstrating sticky panicle axis/sheath and identifiable mature spikelets, plus scale-backed collar and crown.
taxa.lookalikes: Other small-spikeleted Eragrostis including E. spectabilis and E. intermedia
taxa.caution: Only one previously accessible photograph showed a diffuse panicle; the signature gummy axis has NOT been seen. Do not activate a lovegrass key state.

source_key.reference: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon, Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas (1999)

taxa.hill_country_key: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), Grasses of the Texas Hill Country: Vegetative Key and Descriptions; individual characters labeled when used

source_supported_morphology.description: Perennial with erect stems approximately 50–100 cm
Leaf blades relatively hairless
Fingerlike or nearly digitate branches, generally close to the axis and densely flowered
Upper glume and margin of lower floret densely covered with long hairs approximately 2–4 mm
Hard knotty perennial base with rounded somewhat hairy lower sheaths and a roughly 1–3 mm truncated membranous ligule

taxa.actually_visible_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: NO SOURCE PIXELS INSPECTED IN RIGHTS-SAFE PHOTO REVIEW
taxa.not_demonstrated_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: SOURCE IMAGES HELD BY RIGHTS; BOTANICAL IDENTIFICATION NOT VERIFIED
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Obtain permission to inspect the original Hays observation or collect a verified new specimen: paired whole rooted plant, mature flowering branch and 1-mm-scaled spikelet hairs.
taxa.lookalikes: Digitaria insularis and D. patens; Hill Country 2015 explicitly warns vegetative material alone is insufficient
taxa.caution: No source pixels visually inspected under the saved rights-safe review; all floral and vegetative statements are literature-only, not Hays evidence.

taxa.hill_country_key: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), Grasses of the Texas Hill Country: Vegetative Key and Descriptions; individual characters labeled when used

source_supported_morphology.description: Perennial dropseed growing in grassy or disturbed ground
Characteristic long white tufts of hairs near sheath tops, approximately 2–4 mm
Panicle about 15–30(–40) cm long and 2–12 cm wide when opened
Panicle often partially enclosed by the top leaf sheath, especially early in flowering
Lemmas are about as long as the spikelet
Hair-fringe ligule roughly 0.5–1 mm with pilose collar margins

taxa.actually_visible_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: NO SOURCE PIXELS INSPECTED IN RIGHTS-SAFE PHOTO REVIEW
taxa.not_demonstrated_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: SOURCE IMAGES HELD BY RIGHTS; BOTANICAL IDENTIFICATION NOT VERIFIED
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: With permission or a fresh verified Hays plant, photograph a flowering head emerging from its sheath plus sheath-summit white hair tufts, true ligule and one scaled ripe spikelet.
taxa.lookalikes: Sporobolus compositus, S. indicus and other panicled dropseeds
taxa.caution: No source pixels visually inspected in the saved review: original observation images were rights-restricted. No species character is specimen-verified.

taxa.hill_country_key: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), Grasses of the Texas Hill Country: Vegetative Key and Descriptions; individual characters labeled when used

source_supported_morphology.description: Low stolon-forming, sod-forming perennial, to roughly 30 cm
Distinctively flattened and keeled sheaths, leaves often creased lengthwise
Very short ring/fringe of hairs
Flowering head has a broad flattened corky axis with spikelets impressed into one side
Spikelets 4–5 mm long, awnless, two-flowered with lower floret sterile/staminate and upper fertile
Leaves borne in two ranks; folded vernation and rooted stolons

taxa.actually_visible_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Broad-bladed mowed sod/turf habit, compatible with commonly planted St Augustine grass.
taxa.not_demonstrated_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Turf scenes do not expose stolon joints, keeled compressed sheath, hair-ring ligule, or unique sunken florets on a corky rachis; research-grade wild tag does not establish spontaneous Hays occurrence.
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Find a flowering plant with a corky one-sided head, true collar hair ring and rooted stolons, and independently record whether it is escaped or merely a maintained lawn.
taxa.lookalikes: Other planted stoloniferous turfgrasses; nonflowering lawns cannot verify this taxon as wild
taxa.caution: All reviewed source images largely show maintained turf. Published Hays collection does not prove sampled iNaturalist turf is a wild population. Establishment remains on hold.

source_key.reference: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon, Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas (1999)

taxa.hill_country_key: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), Grasses of the Texas Hill Country: Vegetative Key and Descriptions; individual characters labeled when used

source_supported_morphology.description: Spikelets approximately 2.5–3 mm long
Often low ground or disturbed moist sites
Ligule absent at the collar (not a membranous flap or tuft of long hairs)
Blades may have conspicuous purple V-like transverse bands; this is variable and not diagnostic alone
Reproductive discrimination must include glumes and lemma surface and awn condition versus other Echinochloa

taxa.actually_visible_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Small tufted/stolonlike grass and short branched, sometimes crowded panicle with small spikelets; one wet-soil observation.
taxa.not_demonstrated_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Panicle architecture and glume/lemma hair/awn details do not conclusively separate E. colona from other Echinochloa and lookalike Paniceae.
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Use one mature Hays specimen to show the actual absence of a ligule and measure several detached spikelets/lemma surfaces; compare with E. crus-galli, E. muricata and E. walteri.
taxa.lookalikes: Echinochloa crus-galli, E. muricata, E. walteri
taxa.caution: Purple leaf bands and generic barnyardgrass panicles are supportive at best, not sufficient for species approval.

source_key.reference: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon, Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas (1999)

taxa.hill_country_key: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), Grasses of the Texas Hill Country: Vegetative Key and Descriptions; individual characters labeled when used

source_supported_morphology.description: Robust perennial, often 0.5–2 m tall, sometimes taller
Short rhizomes, hard knotty base and persistent perennial growth
Prominently swollen stem nodes, with forward-pointing hairs
Short ciliate ligule around 0.5–1 mm
Spikelets approximately 2.4–3.4 mm
source_supported_morphology.source: FNA older Panicum antidotale account as cited in existing priority file

source_supported_morphology.description: Lower floret staminate and upper fertile; verify both on same dissected spikelet
source_supported_morphology.source: FNA older Panicum antidotale account as cited in existing priority file

taxa.actually_visible_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Excellent close panicles, mature spikelets, culm nodes, leaves and collar on one specimen.
taxa.not_demonstrated_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Exact glume/lemma measurements and spontaneous establishment versus forage planting still need review.
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: Photograph the same Hays plant's rhizomes, distinctive swollen hairy nodes, ligule and fully separated spikelet glumes/florets; resolve planted forage versus spontaneous stand.
taxa.lookalikes: Panicum hallii, P. bergii and other broad-panicled grasses
taxa.caution: Eight previously viewed source images strongly support nodes and panicles, but one observation and no rhizome/floret dissection; species and establishment remain provisional. Keep historical Panicum antidotale alias.

source_key.reference: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon, Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas (1999)

taxa.hill_country_key: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), Grasses of the Texas Hill Country: Vegetative Key and Descriptions; individual characters labeled when used

source_supported_morphology.description: Usually glabrous tufted perennial, approximately 30–75 cm tall
Compact flowering panicles generally 5–10 cm long
Glumes and lemmas thin and papery, often pink-tinged
Lemma apex deeply cleft, a major diagnosis for this taxon
Genus Tridens has multi-flowered spikelets, often 4–12 florets; genus-level context only

taxa.actually_visible_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Dense pale tan to slightly pink compressed flowering panicles, green stems and tufted field habit across separate observations.
taxa.not_demonstrated_in_prior_hays_photo_rev: Thin papery pink-tinged glumes and the deeply cleft lemma apex needed to separate pink tridens not resolved.
taxa.next_same_specimen_proof: On a Hays voucher, separate and backlight an actual ripe lemma tip to reveal the deep cleft; measure panicle and glume dimensions and compare Tridens flavus and T. muticus.
taxa.lookalikes: Tridens flavus, Tridentopsis mutica, other compact Tridens
taxa.caution: Pink-tinged crowded panicles support a preliminary grouping; the diagnostic lemma cleft has not been seen in the earlier Hays photographs.
